name: Sarecycline (Seysara)

lead: Sarecycline (Seysara) is an oral tetracycline antibiotic approved by the FDA in October 2018 for inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne in people aged 9 and older. People take it to clear red, inflamed breakouts on the face and, often, the body.

It blocks bacterial protein synthesis and was designed as a narrow-spectrum drug aimed mainly at the skin bacterium Cutibacterium acnes, with little activity against common gut bacteria, which differs from older tetracyclines like doxycycline and minocycline. Safety and efficacy data from the pivotal trials are summarised in published reviews.

paras: It is a once-daily tablet taken under a prescriber's supervision. Guidelines for oral acne antibiotics generally advise keeping courses to about three months because of resistance concerns.

As a tetracycline-class antibiotic it is prescription-only and used under medical supervision. Antibiotic resistance is a recognised concern with any oral acne antibiotic, which is why courses are time-limited.

angle.text: Sarecycline is a once-daily prescription tetracycline that targets acne bacteria and inflammation, so fewer inflamed lesions appear on the face and body. It was approved for moderate to severe inflammatory acne in 2018 and has been studied in acne trials.

lead: Sarecycline, sold in the United States under the brand name Seysara, is an oral tetracycline-class antibiotic prescribed for acne vulgaris. For people who care about how their skin looks, its job is to calm inflamed red pimples and pustules on the face, chest and back, so that the skin looks clearer and less irritated. The FDA approved the tablet in early October 2018 for the inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne in patients aged 9 and older [1][2].

It was developed by Paratek and Allergan and later acquired by the dermatology-focused company Almirall [1]. It is a narrow-spectrum tetracycline, aimed mainly at Cutibacterium acnes with little activity against the Gram-negative bacteria typical of the human gut [2]. Two identically designed phase 3 trials, which together involved about 2,000 participants, supported approval; in them, sarecycline reduced inflammatory facial lesion counts by more than placebo over 12 weeks [2][3].

Sarecycline is a conventional prescription acne medicine rather than a product that originated in looksmaxxing culture. Its place in the wiki reflects the position of oral antibiotics among options for acne, a common concern in skin-focused appearance discussions, and the 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline gives it a conditional recommendation [4].

paras: The approved indication is the inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne vulgaris in patients aged 9 and older [1][2]. Its label does not cover non-inflammatory lesions (comedones) as a treatment target.
Small investigator-run studies have registered the drug for other skin conditions, including rosacea and perioral (periorificial) dermatitis, and for truncal acne [5][6][7]. These are off-label uses.

In the phase 2 study, sarecycline at two of the three weight-based doses cut inflammatory lesions by about 52 percent from baseline at week 12, versus 38 percent with placebo [8]. In the two phase 3 trials (SC1401 and SC1402), the absolute change in facial inflammatory lesion count at week 12 was -15.3 for sarecycline versus -10.1 for placebo in one trial and -15.7 versus -10.7 in the other, with higher percent reductions in the sarecycline groups [3]. A once-daily weight-based dose of 1.5 mg/kg was the dose studied in the pivotal pair [9].

A pooled analysis of the two phase 3 trials examined truncal acne. Investigator Global Assessment success on the chest was 33.4 percent with sarecycline versus 20.8 percent with placebo at week 12, and on the back 33.1 versus 21.9 percent, with differences already apparent from week 3 [10]. A 2021 registered study, the Patient-reported Outcomes for Sarecycline Effectiveness and Safety (PROSES) trial, enrolled 300 participants with acne and has been completed [11]. The AAD guideline lists sarecycline among options conditionally recommended for acne, alongside oral minocycline, combined oral contraceptives and spironolactone [4].

In the label's safety data, nausea was the only reaction occurring in at least 1 percent of patients, in 3.1 percent of sarecycline patients versus 2.0 percent on placebo, and fewer than 1 percent of women had vulvovaginal candidiasis [12]. Reviews of the pivotal trials and a family-physician guide summarise tolerability [3][13].

The label warns that use during tooth development (the second and third trimesters of pregnancy, infancy and childhood to age 8) may cause permanent yellow-gray-brown tooth discoloration, that the drug can cause fetal harm, that it can increase sunburn so sun and tanning beds should be minimised, and that intracranial hypertension can occur, with isotretinoin co-use to be avoided [12]. The label states that efficacy beyond 12 weeks and safety beyond 12 months have not been established, and that it is not for treating infections [12].

Sarecycline inhibits bacterial protein synthesis. Unlike earlier tetracyclines, its long C7 side chain reaches toward the bacterial messenger RNA and forms hydrogen bonds with nucleotides [2]. It targets clinically relevant Gram-positive organisms, chiefly C. acnes, with little or no activity against typical Gram-negative gut bacteria [2].

Sarecycline has the molecular formula C24H29N3O8 and a molar mass of about 487.5 g/mol. One reported synthesis starts from sancycline and proceeds through palladium-catalysed carbonylation and reductive amination, with an overall yield of about 23% [2].

Sarecycline began as an effort to design a tetracycline specifically for acne rather than for infections generally. The drug carries the development codes P-005672 and WC-3035 [2][3]. A phase 2 dose-ranging study, published in 2018, randomized 285 patients aged 12 to 45 to three weight-based doses or placebo for 12 weeks [8]. Two phase 3 trials followed, SC1401 and SC1402, and the FDA approved the tablet in October 2018, with US availability planned for January 2019 [1]. A capsule formulation had also been studied in the United States but without recent development reported [1]. Paratek and Allergan developed it, and Almirall later acquired it [1].
Sarecycline is prescription-only in the United States [2].
Seysara is the brand name. The compound was previously known by the code P-005672 [2].

Human trials exist. Two phase 3 randomized trials supported the 2018 US approval [1][2], and a systematic review has summarised the published trial literature [14]. Later registered studies include PROSES in 300 acne patients, a 10-person truncal acne study, a 100-participant pilot study in rosacea and a 9-participant study in perioral dermatitis [5][6][7][11].

timeline.event: Phase 2 dose-ranging results published; FDA approves Seysara tablets in early October [1][8].
Tablets planned for US availability in January [1].
Pooled truncal-acne analysis published; PROSES patient-reported-outcomes study begins [10][11].
AAD acne guideline gives sarecycline a conditional recommendation [4].
